boricj · Nov 21, 2026

Compute speed has been outpacing memory speed for decades now. So when you spend the cycles to fetch a cache line (64 bytes generally), you want to milk it for all its worth, to minimize time spent waiting on memory.

On a cold cache, you pay for each level of indirection, so you want to increase fan-out as much as possible. B-trees do that intrinsically.

The data structure is not a pure B+tree. They also strip common key prefix for node elements and store 4 bytes of remaining key data together with a pointer to the children to avoid key lookup in many cases. Plus they tune node sizes to match jemalloc allocation classes to minimize allocation overhead. I am not sure with such focus on cache friendliness the advantage of skip lists for writes still holds as they will still have more cache misses even on inserts.

dreamcompiler · Nov 21, 2026

> Every node carries a backward pointer

Curious. Skiplists don't need back pointers. You can traverse a skiplist backward almost as fast as forward if you keep the "finger" around. The finger is the set of nodes from level-n down to level-0 that point as close to the goal node as possible without going beyond it. The ideal place to keep these nodes is on the stack. To traverse backwards, you do a conventional search for the starting node but every time you go down a pointer level, you push the last pointer on the stack first. Then back traversal becomes stack pops together with appropriate forward recursive calls when you pop back to a pointer that was too far to the left.

It's easier to convey the idea with code than english but I'm not typing the algorithm with my thumbs into my phone.

Is your implementation also a B+ tree? If so how does it use tens of percentage less memory? less metadata?

antirez · Nov 21, 2026

It uses two techniques: B+ tree instead of sorted sets, but also the hash table side, the dictionary, is specialized for sorted sets and stores several items per allocation. The B+ tree leaves hold all the members and scores (also in clusters of many elements, 96 max or 4k: that's a big part of the win), rank lookup can skip many children because of meta data, which is part of the ability to go as fast or faster than Redis even if the memory is so much smaller. The hash table points to leaves in the B+ tree, does not have elements at all, and is heavily optimized to do just the minimum, a single byte tag is used as a speed optimization to optimized lookups in an optimistic way. Basically it is the sum of many different techniques conceived during the years and never adopted for fear of complexity (today no longer a problem), and newely discovered techniques.

P.S. I tried several variants with different representations, so this specific implementation is the Pareto frontier in speed/size of many, many attempts.
